title: I just bought my first property. When can I buy the second?
excerpt: A first-time buyer who prepared well wants a second property this year and worries banks or the tax office will object. Sean explains how rent counts as income, and why subsales speed things up.

question.asker: From C, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: C spent months watching Sean's videos, viewing projects, listing pros and cons and preparing his loan documents before signing the SPA for his first property two weeks ago; his loan offer came in three days. He now wants to buy a second property this year.
question.text: Will banks see a second purchase this year as too aggressive, will the tax office come asking, and how can he improve his chances?

answer.quote: We can declare rent that we collect as income.
answer.summary: Banks and the tax office don't mind how many properties you buy; they care whether you can repay and where your money comes from. If the first property is rented out, its rent can count as income for the next loan after about six months of records, so a rented subsale can lead to a second purchase quickly. If it's your home, the instalment simply reduces what you can borrow.

reasons.title: Rent can add to your borrowing power
reasons.body: With a tenancy agreement and at least six months of rent paid into your account, some banks count 100% of the rent as income and others 80%. A RM2,000 instalment with RM2,200 rent leaves you better off for the next loan, not worse.

reasons.title: Tax is on profit, not rent
reasons.body: Declared rent is taxable, but loan interest and other costs can be deducted, and in the first years most of the instalment is interest. The authorities mainly want to see where your money came from, such as an inheritance or gift.

reasons.title: Subsales move faster than new launches
reasons.body: A subsale completes in about four to six months and can be let straight away, so its rent starts counting sooner. A new launch takes four to five years to complete, which is a long wait before the next step.

reasons.title: The rules can tighten
reasons.body: Two 90% loans per person, low upfront payments and current RPGT rates are policies, not permanent features. Earlier rules differed and future ones could be stricter, which is a reason to act while the terms are favourable.

actions: Rent out the first property if you can live elsewhere cheaply, such as with family.
Keep the tenancy agreement and make sure rent is paid into your bank account every month.
Declare the rental income and keep records of interest and costs to deduct.
Budget about 18% of the price in cash for a subsale, plus about RM50,000 to RM80,000 to furnish it.
Keep six to eight months of expenses and your insurance in place before taking on a second loan.
caveat: Sean thinks most people only need two or three properties in a lifetime, not dozens. If the first purchase is your home, expect to wait for your income to grow before the second.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #211. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures and rules are as Sean stated them in May 2023; check current bank and EPF rules. The episode was sponsored by Dreame, an unrelated vacuum cleaner brand.
